meta.label: Reusable nappies
tradeoffLabels: cheapest over two and a half years
meta.attribution: Prices are quoted from each brand's own site on the date shown, for a single nappy or the stated bundle; nobody's actual cost depends only on unit price, since a full-time cloth user needs a stock of 15 to 25 nappies to get through laundry cycles, so figures that state a full-supply cost (GroVia, Little Lamb) are noted separately from single-item prices. The environment score for every system leans on the UK Environment Agency's 2008 updated lifecycle assessment of nappies, which found that a reusable nappy's manufacture matters less than how it is washed and dried: its baseline scenario put reusable nappies at about the same carbon footprint as a 2006 disposable, full loads and line-drying cut that by up to 40 percent below disposables, and washing at 90C plus tumble-drying every load raised it as much as 75 percent above the baseline. That study did not test individual brands, so scores here describe how a system's fabric and design (bulkier bamboo fitteds dry slower than thin cotton prefolds; a hybrid that is washed less often per change uses less water) interact with that same laundering evidence, not an independent test of the brand itself. Disposable nappies are a separate decision in this catalogue. Not medical or safety advice. Reviewed 2026-08. Suggest changes via Contribute.

criteria.label: Cost per nappy or full supply

products.name: TotsBots Bamboozle (fitted + wrap)

economical.note: TotsBots' own product page lists the Bamboozle nappy, the absorbent inner, at $25.00; the page states it must be 'teamed up with the matching bamboozle waterproof wraps' to work, which are sold separately, so this price does not cover a full change.

accessibility.note: The product page describes 'plush, heavy-duty bamboo fabric' with stretchy tabs and adjustable poppers, but as a two-part fitted-and-wrap system it takes an extra step at every change compared with an all-in-one nappy, and the page gives no washing or drying guidance.

environment.note: The Environment Agency's 2008 study found reusable nappy laundering choices, not manufacture, drive most of the impact, with a baseline scenario around 570kg CO2 equivalent over two and a half years versus about 550kg for a 2006 disposable; a bulky bamboo fitted nappy like this one takes longer to line-dry than a thin cotton prefold, so a household relying on a tumble dryer for it sits closer to the study's higher-impact scenarios.

products.description: A two-part bamboo fitted nappy and wrap system; the absorbent inner alone costs more per piece than most other systems here, and a wrap is an added cost.

products.name: GroVia O.N.E.

economical.note: GroVia's own product page prices the O.N.E. at $24.95 each and states plainly that for full-time use 'you will spend between $550 - $600' on a complete supply, one of the few brands here to give a total cost rather than only a unit price.

accessibility.note: The page describes a 'modular snap in no-prep soaker system' built into a single all-in-one shell, closer to a disposable's one-piece use than a two-part fitted-and-wrap system, though the page also recommends washing every two days.

environment.note: GroVia's own materials list names a '100% Polyester Microfiber' hidden inner layer and a polyester-microfleece-topped cotton soaker, synthetic fabrics rather than the cotton or bamboo the Environment Agency study assumed; the study's finding that wash temperature and drying method drive most of the footprint still applies regardless of fabric.

products.description: A one-piece hybrid nappy with swap-in soaker pads; GroVia's own page is unusual in stating a full two-and-a-half-year supply cost outright rather than leaving buyers to work it out.

products.name: Charlie Banana 2-in-1

economical.note: Charlie Banana's own collection page lists reusable cloth diapers from $11.99 to $129.99 depending on pack size and design; the shell is reused across many changes, with only the insert changed each time.

accessibility.note: The brand's own page states 'you can choose between our washable, reusable inserts or opt for disposable inserts for quick and easy cleanups, all using the same diaper shell cover,' letting a household switch to near-disposable convenience for outings or childcare without buying a second system.

environment.note: When used with its reusable insert, this system follows the same wash-and-dry-driven footprint the Environment Agency study describes for shaped nappies; switching to the brand's disposable insert option for some changes reduces how much is laundered but reintroduces single-use waste for those changes.

products.description: A reusable shell that takes either a washable insert or a disposable one, giving a household the option to fall back to disposable-level convenience without switching systems.

products.name: ALVABABY pocket nappy

economical.note: ALVABABY's own product page lists its one-size solid-colour pocket diaper at $5.69, the cheapest single branded nappy in this comparison by a wide margin.

accessibility.note: The page describes a 'pocket design' that must be stuffed with an insert before use, an extra step compared with an all-in-one, and a polyester outer with 'faux suede cloth inside' that the page says draws moisture away; no washing or drying guidance is given on the page.

environment.note: The shell is polyester with a waterproof, breathable TPU layer, a synthetic construction rather than the cotton or bamboo the Environment Agency study modelled, and the product page discloses no third-party certification; the study's finding that washing and drying practice matters more than fabric still governs its footprint in use.

products.description: An imported budget pocket nappy, by far the cheapest branded single nappy here, with no third-party certification disclosed on its own product page.

products.name: Disana wool cover

economical.note: Green Mountain Diapers lists the Disana Wool Pull-On Cover, made by Disana in Germany, at $42.95 for most sizes; a wool cover is worn over a separate absorbent layer, so this price does not include the nappy itself.

accessibility.note: The retailer's page for this Disana cover says 'HAND WASH AND FLAT DRY ONLY. Do not put it in the dryer,' and that it must be felted by hand before first use, more manual effort per wash than any machine-washable system in this comparison, even though washing itself is needed only rarely.

environment.note: The same page states wool covers need washing only infrequently, 'sometimes only once a month,' far below the weekly-or-more wash cycle the Environment Agency study assumed for shaped nappies and wraps, so the electricity and water use per month is much lower even before accounting for hand-washing instead of a machine.

products.description: A merino wool cover worn over a separate absorbent nappy; it needs washing only about once a month, but every wash is by hand, and it is one more purchase on top of the nappy underneath it.

products.name: Cloth-eez prefold + cover

economical.note: Green Mountain Diapers lists a dozen Cloth-eez prefold diapers at a sale price of $32.95, or about $2.75 each; the page notes this is 'the inner absorbent part of the diaper system' and 'requires a cover (sold separately),' so the true per-change cost is higher once a cover is added.

accessibility.note: The page describes '100% cotton exclusive of trim' in a '4-8-4 ply' construction that must be folded and fastened, then paired with a separate waterproof cover, the most hands-on system in this comparison alongside terry squares.

environment.note: A thin, unbleached cotton prefold like this one dries far faster on a line than a bulky fitted or all-in-one nappy, closer to the Environment Agency study's best-case line-drying scenario, which cut the baseline footprint by 16 percent on its own; the product is also 'Chlorine-free Oeko-Tex 100 certified.'

products.description: The traditional folded-cotton nappy, cheapest per piece of any absorbent layer in this comparison, but the most fiddly to use and sold without the cover it needs.

products.name: Esembly Inner + Outer bundle

economical.note: Esembly's own site prices its organic cloth diaper starter bundle, an Inner and an Outer, at $57.

accessibility.note: The product page describes the Inner as having 'built-in snaps for fast, foolproof closure' paired with a waterproof Outer, and states 'machine drying recommended,' a simpler routine than the hand-wash-only or fold-and-pin systems in this comparison.

environment.note: Esembly's page states the Inner is '100% unbleached Organic Cotton' and the Outer is '100% GRS certified upcycled polyester TPU (derived from recycled plastic bottles),' both OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified; recommending machine drying rather than requiring it leaves room for the line-drying practice the Environment Agency study found most beneficial.

products.description: An organic-cotton inner paired with a recycled-plastic waterproof outer, both independently certified, at a mid-range price for a starter bundle rather than a single nappy.

products.name: Pop-in All-in-Two

economical.note: Close Parent's own collection page prices Pop-in All-in-Two bamboo nappies between £10.99 and £22.55 per nappy; because the waterproof shell separates from the absorbent part and is reused across several changes before it needs washing, fewer shells are needed than in a system where the whole nappy is washed every time.

accessibility.note: The page describes the nappy and wrap as 'connected, but you can take them apart,' an all-in-two design meant to combine the convenience of an all-in-one with the ability to reuse the shell, closer to disposable-style ease than a fully separate two-part system.

environment.note: Bamboo fabric, used for this nappy's absorbent layer, takes longer to dry than thin cotton, but because the shell is not washed at every change, the Pop-in system needs fewer total wash loads over the same period than nappies washed as one piece every time, which the Environment Agency study found was one of the largest levers on footprint.

products.description: A bamboo all-in-two nappy whose waterproof shell separates from the absorbent part and can be reused for more than one change, cutting the number of wash loads needed.

products.name: Little Lamb day and night complete kit

economical.note: Little Lamb's own product page lists this complete kit, 15 one-size pocket nappies, 10 bamboo fitted nappies, 5 wraps, a nappy pail, a wet bag, boosters, wipes and liners, at a regular price of £594.00 and a sale price of £415.00, one of the few full two-and-a-half-year supply prices stated outright in this comparison.

accessibility.note: The kit combines one-size pocket nappies with fitted nappies and includes a nappy pail and wet bag, so a household does not need to separately research and buy those pieces; the page's own washing guidance calls for 'a full, long cycle at 40 or 60 degrees.'

environment.note: The same page recommends 'line drying in direct sunshine' as best, or drying 'near, but not touching, a heat source like a radiator,' the line-drying practice the Environment Agency study found could cut a reusable nappy's footprint by 16 percent against its baseline, though the kit's bamboo fitted nappies will still dry more slowly than a thin cotton prefold.

products.description: A turnkey day-and-night kit combining pocket and fitted nappies with the pail and wet bag a household would otherwise buy separately, priced as a full two-and-a-half-year supply rather than per nappy.

products.name: Secondhand cloth nappies

economical.note: The charity NCT's own page on its Nearly New Sales, which it says help parents sell and recycle 'over 200,000 preloved items every year,' describes buyers picking up secondhand baby and children's essentials at 'around a quarter to a third of the price' of buying new; the page does not price cloth nappies specifically, but nappies are among the reusable baby goods commonly resold through this and similar secondhand channels.

environment.note: The Environment Agency's study modelled reusing a household's own nappies on a second child and found it lowered the lifetime footprint by about 6 percent versus buying new for each child, because the manufacturing impact is spread across more use; the same logic applies to buying a nappy secondhand from another family rather than new, since the manufacturing footprint the study says exceeds a disposable nappy's landfill impact has already been spent.

products.description: Buying used cloth nappies through a resale marketplace, a nearly-new sale, or a swap group; condition and hygiene depend entirely on the seller, which no score here can capture.

products.name: Cloth nappy library or trial kit

economical.note: Real Nappies for London's own page on cloth nappy libraries says they let a family 'try before you buy' and that 'most offer nappy kit loans on a monthly or weekly basis, some even offer long term loans,' run mostly by volunteers who are parents with experience of cloth nappies; the page does not state a loan fee, but describes loan kits rather than a purchase.

products.description: Borrowing a trial kit from a volunteer-run nappy library before buying anything, so a family can compare fitted, pocket and all-in-one systems on their own baby first. A loan, not a permanent supply, so it does not replace choosing and buying a system.

products.name: Council reusable nappy voucher or laundry service subsidy

economical.note: Real Nappies for London's own site states residents in participating boroughs can 'claim a voucher worth up to £70 to help with the upfront cost of buying reusable nappies or put towards a washable nappy laundry service'; other UK councils outside London run comparable schemes, but eligibility and amounts vary by local authority and this scheme is limited to specific London boroughs.

accessibility.note: Because the same voucher can be put toward a nappy laundry service instead of nappies themselves, a family can pay someone else to collect and wash dirty nappies weekly, removing the laundering step the Environment Agency study identified as the main driver of a reusable nappy's cost and effort in use, though only where a participating laundry service operates.

products.description: A council voucher that offsets the cost of buying any of the systems above, or that can instead pay toward a weekly nappy laundry service so a household does not do the washing itself; available only in some UK local authority areas.
